blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A utility trims its circuits on a five-year cycle, and the miles due are about the same every year. To free money, management skips one year's trimming entirely. What happens to that year's trim work, following the lesson?

options.text: It is saved for good, since those circuits now wait a full cycle
options.says: Deferring saves nothing: the deferred circuits are still due and are trimmed the next year.

options.text: It is spread evenly across every remaining year of the cycle
options.says: In the lesson's example the deferred miles all land in the next year (153 miles), and the lump returns a cycle later.

options.text: It lands on the next year, which carries about twice the usual work
options.says: Right: as with C03 and C04, the deferred work joins the next year's, about double a normal year.

options.text: It drops out of the plan, since the standard covers only transmission
options.says: Whatever the standard covers, the work stays due: deferring moves cost and risk into later years, it does not remove them.

origin.section: Vegetation Work Comes Back on a Cycle, So Deferring It Moves Work, Not Removes It

questions.stem: A utility adds a fourth fleet to its portfolio: gas main replacements, done by gas crews that cannot do electric work, with a known number of crew-months per year. Following the lesson, which rows does the crew limit add?

options.text: One crew row per year that sums the gas fleet's work alone
options.says: Right: crews are not shared between fleets, so a crew limit is a row per program and per year.

options.text: One crew row per year that sums the work of every fleet together
options.says: A tree crew does not rebuild towers, and a gas crew does no electric work: the lesson writes one row per program.

options.text: One alternative row per gas main, like the transmission options
options.says: An alternative row groups the options for one asset; it says nothing about crews.

options.text: No row at all, since crews never bind once the budget is met
options.says: The lesson says a crew row binds a fleet on its own even when the money is there; vegetation asks 25 crew-months against 18.

origin.section: Each Fleet Brings Its Own Rows to the Model

questions.stem: A planner compares a $5,000k rebuild of a 230 kV line with a $5,000k set of 12 kV feeder jobs. Following the lesson, how can the two differ in who reviews their cost?

options.text: Both go only to the state commission, like every other utility cost
options.says: FERC sets the rates for most bulk power transmission, so the line rebuild may go to a federal regulator.

options.text: Neither is reviewed, since both are below the N-1 planning limit
options.says: N-1 is a reliability planning rule, not a cost limit, and the lesson says transmission work may be reviewed by its own regulator.

options.text: The feeder jobs go to NERC, and the line rebuild to the state
options.says: NERC writes reliability standards; lines of 34.5 kV or less are almost always under state regulation.

options.text: The line's rates may be set federally, the feeders' by the state
options.says: Right: FERC sets the rates for most bulk transmission, and distribution is regulated by the state commission.

origin.section: Transmission Moves Bulk Power, So Its Projects Are Few, Large and Long
